(Fictional case study for training. Not a real investigation.)

Executive summary

What happened

At 02:47:12 on 12/08/2026, a 220 t class rigid haul truck, HT-407, descending the main ramp of the Stage 4 pit at Bindarra Gold Mine empty struck the right side of a light vehicle, LV-118, coming out of the RL 312 dewatering spur. Times in this report are local time (UTC+8). The truck had braked from 37 km/h and hit at 24 km/h. It pushed the light vehicle 18.4 m down the ramp and rolled it onto its left side against the inner windrow.

The light vehicle driver, a grade control technician, was seriously injured, with a fractured left clavicle, three fractured left ribs and a small pneumothorax. The driver was conscious throughout, was extricated through the rear of the vehicle 27 minutes after the collision and was flown out at 07:40. LV-118 was destroyed. The truck was damaged at the front left and returned to service on 14/08/2026. The Stage 4 pit stood down for 9 hours 15 minutes and the main ramp below RL 340 was closed for 22 hours. [NOT ESTABLISHED: injury status of the haul truck operator]

What the investigation found

[NOT ESTABLISHED: the investigator's probable cause statement]

Two vehicles met at an intersection that was on no mine document, and neither driver knew of the other until the truck came over the crest, with 53 m of view to the light vehicle's beacon. The intersection had 41 m of sight line against a 96 m stopping distance, carried no sign or control, was missing from the in-cab road network and sat inside a suppressed collision awareness geofence. The sight line very likely contributed to this, and the lack of a stop control or warning sign likely contributed to the light vehicle driving out without a full stop. That driving out was extremely likely to have contributed to the collision, because without that vehicle on the ramp there is no collision.

The spur began as a works order classed as routine earthworks, so no management of change record was raised and none of its three referrals was made. This very likely contributed to the missing controls and the suppressed alerts. The positive-call list was drawn only from the annual review, which very likely contributed to neither driver calling. The geofence extension was probably unknown to operators and likely contributed through the expectation that a quiet system meant an empty ramp. The gatehouse issued access cards with no check of the pit driving assessment, which likely contributed, and the guideline's lack of a review trigger likely contributed as well, held at the standard of proof and no higher.

Two conditions worked. The truck operator braked and steered right within 1.4 seconds of the beacon coming into view, so the impact was at 24 km/h and not 37 km/h, and the roll-over protection structure and seatbelt held. Whether airborne dust affected the sighting, and whether the operator's fatigue affected performance, could not be settled. The fourteen night roster and the nine minute night shift extrication wait were unlikely to have contributed, though each increased risk.

What can be done

Operators should treat any new intersection on a haul road, however it is built, as a change needing referral to those who own the traffic plan, the in-cab map and the proximity system, and should make suppression of a safety control known to the people it affects.

The Mining Manager directed at 05:10 on 12/08/2026 that a positive call is required at every Stage 4 intersection until further notice. The spur was barricaded, two of ten other unlisted roads were closed pending a stop control, and suppressed proximity events were added to the monthly collision awareness report. Open recommendations, due 30/09/2026, cover the works order exclusion, a route onto the positive-call list between reviews and change control for geofences.

Factual information

History of the occurrence

The RL 312 dewatering spur was a 240 m access road cut under works order WO-26-4471 to reach dewatering bore DW-14. The works order was raised on 28/07/2026 and the earthworks were recorded complete on 31/07/2026. The bore was energised and the spur first used by light vehicles on 02/08/2026. A "ROAD CLOSED - CONSTRUCTION" sign that had stood at the spur mouth was removed the same day, and nothing was installed in its place. No sign, give-way control or delineation was added afterwards.

At about 22:10 on 04/08/2026 a dewatering technician came out of the spur about 60 m in front of a descending haul truck, reversed back into the spur and let the truck pass. The technician submitted hazard report HAZ-2026-0917 at 23:48 the same night. The Dewatering Superintendent closed it on 06/08/2026 with an entry recording a reminder to the crew at the pre-start of 05/08. The risk rating was reduced from Medium to Low on closure.

The light vehicle driver's site access card was issued on 09/08/2026 after a 20 minute gatehouse briefing, and the first of the driver's three night shifts at Bindarra began that evening.

On the night of the occurrence, dispatch called Stage 4 back to work from crib at 02:22:41. HT-407, a 220 t class rigid haul truck, completed one cycle and was descending the main ramp empty on its second. The light vehicle, LV-118, had one occupant, a grade control technician employed by a survey subcontractor. The technician finished a set of levels at the DW-14 collar and drove the 240 m of spur towards the main ramp, reaching the mouth at about 02:47. These movements rest on the driver's account alone, and the driver's own estimate of "about ten to three" is later than the recorded collision and is not used. The driver said that, at the spur mouth, the driver slowed, looked right up the ramp, saw nothing and drove out, turning right to go up the ramp. The driver put the speed coming out at about 25 km/h and did not believe the vehicle had come to a complete stop. On read-back the driver corrected an earlier statement of having stopped.

The truck's last steady data point was at 02:47:06.0, at 37 km/h and 53 m above the spur mouth. At 02:47:07.4, 38.5 m above the mouth, service brake pressure rose from 0 to 620 kPa in 0.4 seconds, the retarder went to maximum and 14 degrees of right steering was applied. At 02:47:09.2 the collision awareness system logged a proximity event at 21.4 m with a closing speed of 32 km/h, and the alert was suppressed. The truck struck the light vehicle at 02:47:12.0 at 24 km/h, 6.2 m into the ramp from the spur mouth and 3.1 m out from the toe of the inner windrow. LV-118 was turning right, across the descending lane, with its right side towards the truck. The truck's front left struck the right side of the light vehicle and pushed it 18.4 m down the ramp. The vehicle went over at 11.2 m and came to rest on its left side against the inner windrow, facing down-ramp. The truck stopped at about 02:47:19, 19 m below the intersection.

The truck operator reported the collision on the pit channel from 02:47:41. Dispatch stopped all Stage 4 traffic at 02:48:01, 49 seconds after the collision, and told the operator to stay in the cab until the ramp was stopped above and below. The operator was released at 02:48:44. The emergency response team was paged at 02:48. The first response vehicle entered the pit at 02:51 and reached the scene at 02:54. The second responder arrived with the hydraulic rescue tool at 03:07. The door on the resting side was against the ground, so the driver was extricated through the rear of the vehicle at 03:14, 27 minutes after the collision. The driver was conscious throughout, reached the surface medical facility at 03:41 and was flown to the metropolitan trauma centre at 07:40.

The Stage 4 pit stood down for 9 hours 15 minutes, and the main ramp below RL 340 was closed for 22 hours. At 05:10 the Mining Manager directed that a positive call on the pit channel was required before entering any intersection in the Stage 4 pit, listed in the traffic management plan or not, until further notice. The spur was barricaded and closed to all traffic.

Injuries and damage

The driver of LV-118 was seriously injured, with a fractured left clavicle, three fractured left ribs and a small pneumothorax. The driver was treated at the surface medical facility and evacuated by air. The occurrence was notified to the State Mines Inspectorate as a reportable injury (ORR-OCC-2026-0332).

[NOT ESTABLISHED: injury status of the haul truck operator]

[NOT ESTABLISHED: whether any other person was injured]

LV-118 was destroyed. Damage was concentrated on the right side from the B pillar forward. The roll-over protection structure was deformed inward at the right rear mounting and was not breached. The driver's seatbelt was found fastened, with loading marks on the webbing. The 4.5 m beacon whip was sheared at its base and its lamp worked when tested.

HT-407 was damaged at the front left bumper, the left mudguard and the lower two steps of the access ladder, with no damage above the bumper line. It returned to service on 14/08/2026.

Personnel information

The haul truck operator had 14 months at Bindarra, 4 years 2 months with Tarrowen Mining Services, 7 years on 220 t class rigid haul trucks and 11 years in open pit mining. The operator's verification of competency on type was issued 06/2025 and was current, and the annual refresher was completed 02/2026. The site general induction was 06/2025. The training file shows no traffic management refresher since that induction. The induction's traffic management module is a 23 slide package that names the nine Appendix B intersections and does not cover what to do at an intersection that is not listed. No training record anywhere on site, for any person, covers the suppression geofences of the collision awareness system. The occurrence was on night 10 of a 14 night swing, 8 hours 47 minutes into a 12 hour 30 minute shift. The operator's voluntary sleep record gave 6 hours 30 minutes of sleep in the preceding day and between 5 and 7 hours on each of the nine days before that.

The light vehicle driver completed a Hallorn general mining induction, a two hour online module, on 24/07/2026. The site access card was issued on 09/08/2026, and the driver worked night shifts on 09/08, 10/08 and 11/08. The training file holds no record of the Bindarra light vehicle pit driving assessment. The driver had never seen BIN-TMP-004. [NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the Bindarra site supplement was issued to the light vehicle driver] [NOT ESTABLISHED: the content of the Bindarra light vehicle pit driving assessment]

The night shift supervisor had 19 years in open pit mining, 8 years with Tarrowen Mining Services and 2 years 6 months in the role, and held current haul truck, excavator and dozer verifications of competency. The supervisor did not know a light vehicle was in the Stage 4 pit that night.

The truck operator and the night shift supervisor were both tested for drugs and alcohol after the occurrence, and both results were negative.

Site and conditions

The occurrence was in darkness. There was no fixed lighting in the Stage 4 pit, the only lighting being vehicle lighting and the light plants at the loading face, 1.1 km away and out of sight behind the crest. Moonset was at 23:18 the previous evening. The Bindarra met station recorded wind from the south-east at 8 km/h, a temperature of 9 degrees and no precipitation. The last recorded rainfall at the site was 26 days earlier.

The main ramp at RL 312 ran approximately north-west on a 9.1 per cent descending grade, 24 m wide between windrows. The surface was dry and well maintained. Traffic keeps left, so a descending truck runs on the open, pit side of the road. The spur joined the ramp on a descending truck's left, on the inside of a left-hand bend, at an included angle of 71 degrees. It met the ramp 34 m below a convex grade break where the descent steepens, which the crews call the crest.

Mine survey pickup SUR-26-1188 of 13/08/2026 gave the following sight distances. An operator at an eye height of 5.80 m first had line of sight to the spur mouth at 41 m, and to the top of a 4.5 m beacon whip on a light vehicle approaching the mouth at 53 m, while the vehicle's body was not in view. A driver at the spur mouth, at an eye height of 1.45 m, first had line of sight to a descending truck at 38 m. The 1.6 m inner windrow stood between the spur and the ramp for the last 25 m of the spur's approach and took the truck's lower body out of view before that. The stopping distance of a 220 t class truck travelling empty at the posted 40 km/h on a 9 per cent descending grade, with the manufacturer's data and a 1.5 second response, is 96 m.

At the time of the occurrence the intersection had no warning sign on either ramp approach, no give-way or stop control at the spur mouth, no delineation and no posted speed for the spur.

The water cart log records the main ramp between RL 280 and RL 400 last watered at 01:10, 1 hour 37 minutes before the occurrence, against a standing night shift instruction of a ramp pass every 90 minutes. The fixed dust monitor on the RL 328 bench beside the ramp, 180 m up-ramp of the intersection and above the grade break, logged PM10 at 142 micrograms per cubic metre in the 02:40 to 02:50 interval, against a shift mean of 88 and a site trigger of 250. That is a measure of airborne particulate at the monitor head. Nothing at Bindarra measures visibility, and no measurement exists of what could be seen from either cab. The investigator examined the ramp surface at 06:20 and found it dry throughout, with no damp patches, ponding or greasy film at or above the intersection.

Recorded data

The fleet management system download from HT-407 (TRW-TS-2026-114) gave a 1.4 second interval between the last steady data point and the first brake pressure rise. Mean deceleration from the brake application to the collision was 0.78 m/s2 net of the grade, from 37 km/h to 24 km/h in 4.6 seconds over 39 m of road. The accelerometer logged 1.9 g longitudinal at impact. The braked tyre scuff began 38.5 m up-ramp of the spur mouth and ran 58 m to the truck's resting position, deviating 1.4 m to the right over its first 20 m. Had no braking been applied, the collision speed would have been 37 km/h. The in-cab road network for the Stage 4 pit was last published on 24/07/2026 and does not contain the spur, so the display showed the main ramp with no intersection at RL 312. LV-118 is not dispatched and carries no fleet management system, and its collision awareness transponder is a passive tag.

The collision awareness system on HT-407 operated at Level 8, operator advisory. Level 9, automated intervention, is available on the fleet and is not enabled at Bindarra. Advisory alerts are raised on a tag entering the 60 m detection ring at a closing rate above 10 km/h, except inside a suppression geofence, where no alert is raised at any range and a proximity event is logged only once the range falls below 25 m. The S4-LOAD geofence was drawn on 14/03/2025 around the Stage 4 loading face and was extended northward on 09/06/2026 when the face advanced, which carried the boundary up the main ramp for the first time. The extended boundary lies 180 m up-ramp of the RL 312 intersection. The extension was made by the contractor's technical services group as a system configuration task and is not recorded in the traffic management plan. [NOT ESTABLISHED: the size of the S4-LOAD extension of 09/06/2026, as the configuration record gives the new boundary and not the old] [NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the technical services group told anyone at Orrabinda or Tarrowen of the June 2026 geofence extension] The event log records a proximity event at 02:47:09.2 at 21.4 m, the impact at 02:47:12.0, and a further proximity event at 02:47:12.1 at 0.0 m, each with the alert suppressed. Outside a geofence, an advisory would have been raised when the tag entered the 60 m ring, at about 02:47:06.5.

Collision awareness statistics for the 12 months to 11/08/2026 show that HT-407 raised 1,684 advisory alerts, every one outside the geofence. Across the Stage 4 haul fleet, 68 proximity events were logged inside the geofence and suppressed. Nine of them involved a light vehicle tag on the main ramp below the boundary, all after 09/06/2026. The technical services group's standing report covers alert counts and system health and does not report suppressed events.

The pit channel was logged continuously (RAD-2026-0332), and the investigator listened to the whole period from the return from crib to two minutes after the collision. HT-407 called, and was acknowledged, at the RL 360 crossover going up at 02:28:10 and coming down at 02:46:21, and at the ROM pad turn-off at 02:37. There was no transmission by either vehicle about the spur, the bore or a light vehicle being in the Stage 4 pit. LV-118 made no transmission on the channel beyond logging on at 18:04 at the start of shift.

Equipment

HT-407 was commissioned in 03/2021 and had 31,480 engine hours. Its last 500 hour service was on 28/07/2026 with no defects carried. The monthly brake performance test on 03/08/2026 gave a mean deceleration of 0.80 m/s2 net in the empty condition on a 9 per cent descending grade. A test on 14/08/2026, before the unit returned to service, gave 0.82. The pre-start check sheet for 11/08/2026 was complete and recorded no defects. No defect was raised against the brakes, retarder, lighting, mirrors, cameras or cab glass in the twelve months before the occurrence.

LV-118 was a 4WD utility in service from 02/2024 with 61,200 km. Its last periodic service was on 17/07/2026. It was fitted with a certified roll-over protection structure, a 4.5 m amber beacon whip, reflective marking to the site standard and a UHF radio. The inspection sheet for the week of 09/08/2026 recorded all items serviceable.

Organisational and management information

Orrabinda Resources operates the mine and its Mining Manager owns the traffic management plan. Tarrowen Mining Services is the haul contractor and its technical services group configures the collision awareness system. Hallorn Survey & Geotechnical employed the light vehicle driver and has held a recognition agreement with Orrabinda Resources since 2023.

Mines Safety Guideline MSG-14 revision 4 was made under Mining Operations Safety Regulations 2018 r 6.22. Clause 3.2 requires the traffic management plan to be reviewed at intervals not exceeding twelve months and after any significant change to the road network, and does not define a significant change. Clause 3.5 provides that the plan is a site document, not approved by the Inspectorate and not submitted to it except on request following an occurrence or inspection. Clause 5.1 requires the operator to nominate the intersections and interaction zones at which positive communication is required, and sets no minimum and no basis. Clause 5.4 requires a light vehicle to be detectable by a heavy vehicle operator, by line of sight, elevated marking, radio communication, a proximity detection system or a combination of these.

BIN-TMP-004 revision 7 was issued on 12/11/2025, with the next review due on 12/11/2026. It provides as follows.

  • Clause 4.1: "Light vehicles shall give way to heavy vehicles at all times and in all circumstances."
  • Clause 4.3.1 requires a positive call on the pit channel before entering any intersection listed at Appendix B, and entry only after the call is acknowledged or the channel is confirmed clear.
  • Clause 4.3.2: "At intersections not listed at Appendix B, vehicles shall give way in accordance with clause 4.1. No call is required."
  • Clause 6.2 requires the available sight distance at every intersection to be not less than the stopping distance of the largest vehicle at the posted speed and in no case less than 120 m, and requires a stop control, signalised control or traffic controller where that cannot be achieved.
  • Clause 6.4 requires a warning sign 50 m in advance on each approach, a give-way control on the minor road and delineation at the mouth, at every intersection shown on the road layout drawing at Schedule 1.
  • Clause 9.1 requires review annually and after any significant change to the road network.

Appendix B lists nine intersections. Appendix B and Schedule 1 are reissued at the annual review, and the plan makes no provision for adding an intersection to either between reviews, or for referring a new road to the plan's owner when it is cut. Schedule 1 is dated 12/11/2025 and the RL 312 spur does not appear on it. Appendix B is reproduced on a laminated board in each crib room, and the Stage 4 board is the 12/11/2025 issue. The measured available sight distance at the intersection was 41 m against a 96 m stopping distance, so it did not meet clause 6.2 on either limb. Clause 6.4 applies to intersections shown on Schedule 1, and the spur is not on it.

Management of Change procedure ORR-PRO-022 clause 5.2 requires a management of change record before a change to the mine's road network. Clause 5.3 excludes routine earthworks under a works order within an approved pit design where no new plant or vehicle type is introduced. Clause 5.4 provides that where a record is raised the impact assessment includes referral to the traffic management plan owner, the survey department for the fleet management system road network, and the contractor's technical services group for the collision awareness system configuration. The works order form at Schedule 4 has no equivalent fields.

WO-26-4471 classified the work as routine earthworks within the approved Stage 4 design and recorded management of change as not required under clause 5.3. It was raised by the Mining Engineer on 28/07/2026 and approved by the Mining Superintendent on 29/07/2026. It carried no scope for signage, no survey pickup, no referral to the plan owner, no request to publish a revised road network and no review of the geofences. Its handover field reads "N/A".

Contractor Management Standard ORR-STD-009 clause 7.3 allows a contractor's own general induction to be accepted as equivalent where the contractor holds a current recognition agreement. Clause 7.4 states that equivalence does not extend to the Bindarra site-specific supplement or the Bindarra light vehicle pit driving assessment, which shall be completed at site by every person who will drive in an operating pit. Clause 7.5 makes the engaging department responsible for verifying that clause 7.4 has been completed before a card is issued. The gatehouse issues cards against the recognition agreement alone, holds no record of either item and is not asked for one. Nothing in the access card system distinguishes a person who may drive in an operating pit from a person who may not. [NOT ESTABLISHED: whether Tarrowen supervisors have been trained on BIN-TMP-004]

The traffic management plan had annual reviews on 14/11/2023, 10/11/2024 and 12/11/2025. No out-of-cycle review has been carried out under clause 9.1 in the plan's eleven year history. The survey department's road register records 14 new roads cut in the Stage 4 pit since the 12/11/2025 review, 11 under a works order and 3 under a management of change record. The 3 were referred to the plan's owner and none of the 11 was.

A search of the reporting system for the 24 months to 11/08/2026 returned four hazard reports describing a light vehicle and a haul truck interacting at an intersection, including HAZ-2026-0917. The other three, from 03/2025, 09/2025 and 02/2026, were at three different locations not listed at Appendix B. All four were closed within three days with an entry recording a reminder to the crew. None was referred to the plan owner and none led to a change to Appendix B, Schedule 1 or any physical control.

Roster and fatigue

The contractor's Stage 4 haul roster is 14 nights on and 7 off, 18:00 to 06:30, a 12 hour 30 minute shift with a 30 minute crib. The contractor's fatigue management standard sets a maximum of 14 consecutive night shifts and a minimum 10 hour break, and both limits were met. Site access records confirm that the previous nine shifts were worked in sequence with none extended beyond 12 hours 40 minutes. The night shift supervisor works the same pattern as the crews supervised.

Emergency response

The night shift is rostered with one qualified mines rescue paramedic, based at the surface medical facility. The second responder, who must be present before any extrication, is called in from the accommodation village 11 km from the gatehouse, in the second response vehicle, which is garaged there and carries the hydraulic rescue tool. The post-incident review found that the extrication was delayed by approximately 9 minutes waiting for the second responder and the tool, measured from 02:58, when the paramedic's primary survey was complete and the extrication plan made, to the second responder's arrival at 03:07. It recorded that the delay did not affect the clinical outcome because the injuries were stable and the patient was conscious throughout.

Interviews and reports

The haul truck operator told investigators that the light vehicle's whip came up over the crest at about forty metres, and that the operator braked and steered in one movement. The operator did not steer left because "it's a hundred and something metres down. Right is the wall." The operator knew the spur had been cut, thought it was still closed and had noticed that the closed sign was gone. The in-cab screen showed "the ramp. Just the ramp." The operator said the collision awareness system had never sounded on the ramp below the crest in fourteen months, assumed that meant the road was empty, and learned from the supervisor afterwards that the system was switched off there. The operator described the calling practice as calls at the listed intersections and none elsewhere. Asked about dust, the operator said there was some hanging around and "I couldn't tell you if it made a difference." Asked about tiredness, the operator said "Tired, the way you are on night ten. Not falling asleep tired." Asked what the investigation should look at, the operator said "Put a sign on it and put it on the map." The survey places the beacon first in view at 53 m, and the operator's figure of about forty metres was an estimate.

The night shift supervisor said in interview that the supervisor did not know a light vehicle was in the pit, and that there was no permit, call-in or record by which that could be known. The supervisor knew the spur had been cut and that the dewatering crew used it, but had never thought of it as an intersection, and could find no mention of it in the pre-start notes for the ten days since it opened. The supervisor said calls were made at the nine intersections on the crib room board and that requiring calls everywhere would make the channel unusable. The supervisor had learned in about mid 2025 that alerts were turned off at the dig, did not know the geofence had been extended in June 2026 or that it now reached the ramp above the spur, and told the truck operator of the suppression after the collision. The supervisor knew of no process for a light vehicle entering an operating pit, and asked for a permit, call-in or record by which a supervisor knows which light vehicles are in the pit.

The haul truck operator also submitted a safety report (ASR-2026-0341) under a confidential reporting scheme. The operator reported in it a matching account of the approach, of not knowing the road was open, of making no call at an unlisted intersection in line with the practice at the mine, and of having taken a quiet collision awareness system to mean an empty pit.

The dewatering technician's hazard report HAZ-2026-0917 stated: "The problem is you cannot see up the ramp from that road. There is a rise in the ramp and a windrow along the side and you are out on the road before you can see anything." It also stated: "The trucks are doing forty coming down empty. I do not think they know the road is there."

The closure entry, made on 06/08/2026 by the Dewatering Superintendent, read: "Trucks have right of way on the ramp per the traffic management plan. No further action required. Closed."

[NOT ESTABLISHED: the State, location and ownership details of the mine beyond the names above]

Analysis

This analysis follows the conditions that built an unreferred intersection into an operating haul road, the controls that did not apply to it, the actions of the two drivers, and the collision and its outcome.

General

Several matters were examined and were not part of the occurrence. The haul truck operator had seven years on 220 t class trucks, a current verification of competency issued 06/2025 and an annual refresher completed 02/2026. Drug and alcohol tests on the operator and the shift supervisor were both negative.

The truck's brakes were not a factor. The monthly test on 03/08/2026 gave 0.80 m/s2 net and the test on 14/08/2026 gave 0.82. The download of the occurrence gives 0.78 over the 4.6 seconds of braking, which is within the scatter of the two tests. No brake, retarder or park brake defect had been raised against the unit in the previous twelve months. It is very unlikely that the service brakes delivered less than their tested deceleration during the stop.

The ramp surface was not a factor. The met station recorded no precipitation, the last rainfall was 26 days earlier and the investigator found the ramp dry throughout at 06:20. The braked scuff ran continuously for 58 m with no sign of a locked wheel, and the deceleration achieved matched the dry figure. It is very unlikely that the surface was wet or slippery.

The light vehicle was serviceable, its beacon lamp worked when tested after recovery, and its inspection sheet for the week of 09/08/2026 recorded all items serviceable. The occurrence was in darkness, with no fixed lighting in the Stage 4 pit.

How the intersection came to exist unreferred

ORR-PRO-022 clause 5.2 requires a management of change record before "a change to the mine's road network". Clause 5.3 excludes "routine earthworks carried out under a works order within an approved pit design, where no new plant or vehicle type is introduced". WO-26-4471 cut 240 m of access road to bore DW-14 and classified it under clause 5.3, with "Management of change not required". Its handover field read "N/A".

The classification removed the three referrals that clause 5.4 attaches to a management of change record: to the traffic management plan owner, to the survey department for the in-cab road network, and to the contractor's technical services group for the collision awareness system geofences. The works order form at Schedule 4 has no equivalent fields. None of the three referrals was made. The in-cab road network published on 24/07/2026 therefore still showed the main ramp with no intersection at RL 312 on the night, and the S4-LOAD suppression geofence, extended up the ramp on 09/06/2026, already covered the place where the spur joined it.

The pattern was not confined to this spur. Of the 14 new roads cut in Stage 4 since the 12/11/2025 review, the 3 raised under a management of change record were referred to the plan's owner and none of the 11 raised under a works order was. Three of the four hazard reports from the previous 24 months that described a light vehicle and a haul truck meeting unexpectedly at an unlisted intersection were closed in the same way as the report of 04/08/2026. Each was closed within three days with a reminder to the crew, and none was referred to the plan owner. The report of 04/08/2026 was closed on 06/08/2026 with its risk rating reduced from Medium to Low. This showed the same absence of any route to the plan's owner, and it is why the spur remained unreferred after a technician had described its hazard in writing.

Opening the spur under a works order, so that nothing was referred to anyone, very likely contributed to the missing stop control and warning sign and to the suppression of collision alerts at the spur. A management of change record would have sent a survey showing the intersection failing the clause 6.2 sight distance rule to the plan's owner, and would have sent the new intersection to the group that configures the geofence. Both referrals are standing parts of the procedure, and the three roads raised under a record were referred. The plan's owner might have left the spur to the annual review, because no out-of-cycle review had been held in the plan's eleven years, so a referral is not in itself a control. This was weighed and did not outweigh the effect of having the two referrals reach the right people.

The guideline's part

MSG-14 clause 3.2 requires the plan to be reviewed within twelve months and after any "significant change to the mine's road network, vehicle fleet or operating pattern", and does not define the term or give an example. Clause 5.1 requires the operator to nominate the intersections at which positive communication is required, and sets no minimum and no basis. Clause 3.5 provides that the plan is a site document that is not approved by the Inspectorate. Bindarra's plan met the guideline on its face, because it had been reviewed within twelve months and nominated nine interaction zones, and the mine was not in breach. Clause 5.4, which allows any one of five means of making a light vehicle detectable, is context and not part of this factor.

It is likely that the guideline contributed. A defined trigger would have required the plan to be reopened when a road was added, and a stated basis for nominating intersections would have given one that failed the sight distance rule a claim on the call list. Against this, clause 9.1 of the plan already allowed an out-of-cycle review at any time, and nothing in MSG-14 prevented the mine from listing every intersection it had. The guideline made inaction the default, but nothing inside the mine put the question in front of the plan's owner, and that failure was the larger part. The conclusion is held at the standard of proof and no higher.

The sight line and the missing controls

BIN-TMP-004 clause 6.2 requires the available sight distance at every intersection to be not less than the stopping distance of the largest vehicle at the posted speed and in no case less than 120 m. Where that cannot be achieved it requires a stop control, signalised control or traffic controller. The survey of 13/08/2026 gave 41 m against a stopping distance of 96 m for an empty 220 t class truck at 40 km/h on a 9 per cent descent, so the intersection met neither limb. A truck at the posted speed could not stop for anything first seen at this intersection, however alert its operator.

The geometry set the sequence. The spur mouth lies 34 m below a convex grade break. The operator first had line of sight to the light vehicle's beacon at 53 m, and to the spur mouth at 41 m, while the driver at the mouth first had line of sight to a descending truck at 38 m, with the 1.6 m windrow hiding the truck's lower body before that. With twice the sight line, the same 1.4 second response and the same braking would have stopped the truck short of the spur. The sight line very likely contributed to neither driver becoming aware of the other until the truck came over the crest. A sight line is only hazardous once something is in it, and the other conditions described here are what put a vehicle in it.

Clause 6.4 requires a warning sign 50 m in advance on each approach, a give-way control on the minor road and delineation at the mouth, but only at intersections shown on the road layout drawing at Schedule 1, and the spur was not on it. The intersection carried no warning sign, no stop or give-way control, no delineation and no posted speed. The "ROAD CLOSED - CONSTRUCTION" sign was removed on 02/08/2026 and nothing replaced it. The hazard report of 04/08/2026 named the missing sign and the missing give-way.

The absence of any stop control or sign probably contributed to the light vehicle driving out of the spur without stopping. A stop control would have held the light vehicle at the mouth while the truck came into view, and a sign on the truck's approach would have told its operator that an intersection lay below the crest. The operator said in interview, "If there'd been a sign on my side of that crest I'd have been at twenty and I'd have been looking for him." On 04/08 a technician who came out of the same spur in front of a truck about 60 m away reversed back and let it pass.

The case against the sign is that the view from the mouth gives only 38 m, about four seconds of a truck at 37 km/h, which is thin even from a standstill. The effect of a sign on the truck rests on the operator's own account after the event, and a sign at an intersection absent from the in-cab map would have been a single cue. These points limit how much weight the contribution can bear and are the reason it is graded no higher.

The positive-call loop

BIN-TMP-004 clause 4.3.1 requires a positive call on the pit channel before entering any intersection listed at Appendix B, and clause 4.3.2 says that at other intersections vehicles give way under clause 4.1 and "No call is required". Appendix B lists nine intersections and is reissued only at the annual review. An intersection is added only where it appears on the Schedule 1 drawing and the review assesses it as needing positive communication. Nothing in the plan allows an addition between reviews, and nothing requires a new road to be referred to the plan's owner. The spur was on neither document.

Neither driver made a call before the intersection. The pit channel was logged continuously and the investigator listened to the whole period. HT-407 called at each listed intersection it passed and was acknowledged, the last at the RL 360 crossover at 02:46:21, 51 seconds before the collision. LV-118 made no transmission after logging on at 18:04. No call was required at the spur, which is not listed. The truck operator, the light vehicle driver and the night shift supervisor each described the same practice independently. Calls are made at the nine intersections on the crib room board and nowhere else, and the supervisor said they had never corrected anyone for not calling elsewhere and that requiring calls everywhere would make the channel unusable.

Listing the spur would very likely have produced a call, because the operator called at every listed intersection the operator passed that night and the channel was open with the light vehicle on it. The way positive calls are required only at listed intersections, and added only at the annual review, therefore very likely contributed to neither driver making a call. A call made and not acknowledged would still have left a driver deciding whether to go. The absence of a call itself probably contributed to neither driver being aware of the other, because a call would have been heard by the other vehicle, by dispatch and by the supervisor. A call gives knowledge and not separation, and the vehicles would still have had to resolve who went first over 41 m of sight line, which is why this is graded below certainty.

The suppressed collision awareness alert

The collision awareness system on the Stage 4 haul fleet operated at Level 8, operator advisory, and raises an alert when a tag enters the 60 m ring at a closing rate above 10 km/h, except inside a suppression geofence. Inside one, no alert is raised at any range and a proximity event is logged only below 25 m. S4-LOAD was drawn on 14/03/2025 to stop nuisance alerts at the loading face. It was extended northward on 09/06/2026 as a configuration task by the contractor's technical services group, which carried the boundary up the main ramp to a point 180 m up-ramp of the intersection. The extension was not recorded in the traffic management plan or reviewed against it. The system logged LV-118 at 21.4 m at 02:47:09.2 and the alert was suppressed.

The system data show this configuration. Nothing records that operators were told. No training record anywhere on site covers the geofences, and the truck operator and the night shift supervisor each said they did not know the system was off on the ramp. The supervisor knew from mid 2025 that alerts were off at the dig and did not know the boundary had been extended up the ramp. Between 09/06/2026 and the occurrence nine proximity events involving a light vehicle on the main ramp below the boundary were logged and suppressed. These and 68 suppressed events in all over twelve months were visible to anyone who queried the system, and nobody had, because the standing report does not include them. It is extremely likely that the alerts were suppressed at the spur and that operators did not know. That the system was suppressed is shown by the system itself, and the "did not know" half rests on two accounts and the absence of any training record or notice. Whether other operators held the same belief as the truck operator is [NOT ESTABLISHED: whether other operators held the same belief about the collision awareness system].

The alert itself would have added little. Unsuppressed, it would have sounded when the tag entered the 60 m ring at about 02:47:06.5, half a second after the beacon came into view and about a second before the brakes went on, and the system is advisory with no intervention. The contribution therefore works through expectation. The operator said in interview, "I assumed there was nothing to go off at", and wrote in the operator's report that a quiet system was taken to mean an empty pit. For the first ten months of the operator's fourteen that was true, because the ramp was outside the geofence. From June the system was silent there whatever was on the road. The operator came over the crest with that expectation and with no intersection on the screen. It is likely that the suppression contributed to the lack of awareness between the drivers, held at the standard of proof and no higher. The effect is real but cannot be measured, and the case against it is that the operator was descending at the speed every operator uses on that ramp and named a sign, not the system, as the operator's own remedy.

The light vehicle entering the ramp

BIN-TMP-004 clause 4.1 requires light vehicles to give way to heavy vehicles "at all times and in all circumstances". The driver described applying that rule. The driver said they slowed at the mouth, looked right up the ramp, saw nothing and drove out, and corrected the account on read-back from "stopped" to "slowed". The driver put the speed coming out of the spur at about 25 km/h and did not believe they had come to a complete stop. The collision awareness log places the light vehicle at the mouth at 02:47:09.2 with the truck 21.4 m above it, and the impact came 2.8 seconds later, 6.2 m into the ramp.

On the recorded times the look came before the truck came over the crest, when it was beyond anything the driver's position allowed them to see. The truck was inside the driver's 38 m of view from about 02:47:07.4, nearly two seconds before the mouth was reached. A stop at the mouth would very likely have shown the truck, as the technician's reversal on 04/08 had done. The light vehicle driving out of the spur without stopping was extremely likely to have contributed, because without the light vehicle on the ramp there is no collision. A stop is only as good as the look from it at 38 m, which is the margin that keeps this just short of certainty. The light vehicle's movements before it reached the mouth rest on the driver's own account alone, and could not be corroborated further.

ORR-STD-009 clause 7.4 requires that the Bindarra site supplement and the light vehicle pit driving assessment "shall be completed at site by every person who will drive a vehicle in an operating pit and shall not be substituted". Clause 7.5 makes the engaging department responsible for verifying this before a card is issued. The gatehouse issued the driver's card on 09/08/2026 against Hallorn's recognition agreement alone after a 20 minute briefing on muster points, speed limits and personal protective equipment. It held no record of either item and was not asked for one, and nothing in the card system distinguishes a person who may drive in an operating pit from one who may not. The driver's training file showed the Hallorn online module and no pit driving assessment, and the driver had never seen BIN-TMP-004.

The issue of cards with no check of the assessment probably contributed to the driver leaving the spur without stopping. The assessment is where a light vehicle driver is taught how to approach an intersection that cannot be seen up, which is to stop and look again and not merely slow. It is held below the other contributions for two reasons. The content of the assessment is not held, and the driver was already applying its first rule of giving way to heavy vehicles. The plan requires no call at an unlisted intersection, so the assessment would not have taught a call at RL 312 and the driver's statement that they would have called if told to cannot be stretched that far. [NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the Bindarra site supplement was issued to the light vehicle driver]

Convergence and impact

HT-407 descended empty at 37 km/h with no intersection on its screen, no warning sign, no call and no alert. LV-118 came out of the spur toward a mouth with 38 m of sight line, no give-way control and no call. The first sighting available to the truck operator was the beacon at 53 m, six seconds before impact, as the survey predicts. Neither the radio log, the download, the collision awareness log nor any interview contains an indication that either driver knew of the other before then. The night shift supervisor did not know a light vehicle was in the pit, and there was no permit, call-in or board by which they could have known. Neither driver being aware of the other until the truck came over the crest was extremely likely to have existed and extremely likely to have led to the collision, because nothing in the six seconds left could have prevented it. This is graded just below certainty because the light vehicle's movements before the mouth rest on the driver's account alone.

The impact was at 24 km/h, 4.6 seconds after the brake application and 6.2 m into the ramp from the spur mouth. The truck's front left struck the right side of LV-118, which was turning right across the descending lane. The truck's accelerometer logged 1.9 g. The light vehicle was pushed 18.4 m down the ramp and went over at 11.2 m, coming to rest on its left side against the inner windrow. The roll-over produced the injuries: a fractured left clavicle, three fractured left ribs and a small pneumothorax.

What worked

The truck operator's response worked. The download gives 1.4 seconds from the beacon coming into view to the rise in brake pressure, inside the 1.5 seconds the plan's own stopping distance calculation assumes. The retarder went to maximum and 14 degrees of right steering was applied in the same movement. Braking from 37 to 24 km/h removed about 58 per cent of the impact energy. The steering input took the truck towards the wall and away from the open edge and a drop of more than 100 m, which kept the push running down the ramp so that the light vehicle came to rest against the pit side windrow. After the collision the operator stayed in the cab on dispatch's instruction until the ramp was stopped, then went down and stayed with the driver until the response team arrived.

The light vehicle's defences worked. The roll-over protection structure was deformed inward at the right rear mounting and was not breached, and the seatbelt was fastened and showed loading marks. Dispatch stopped all Stage 4 traffic 49 seconds after the collision, and the driver was conscious throughout.

Matters considered and not found contributing

The wet or slippery ramp and the service brake degradation are dealt with under General and were not found to contribute.

The roster of fourteen consecutive 12.5 hour night shifts was examined as an organisational factor. The operator was on night 10 of 14, 8 hours 47 minutes into the shift and in the window of lowest circadian alertness. Every limit in the contractor's fatigue standard was met. It is unlikely that the roster contributed to this occurrence, because the one mechanism it could have worked through, a slow or absent response, is contradicted by the download. The response of 1.4 seconds was inside the plan's allowance, and the braking and steering that followed were correct and immediate. Braking at 0.78 m/s2 from 53 m with a response time of zero still ends in a collision, at about 17 km/h instead of 24, so the 1.4 seconds cost about 7 km/h of impact speed and not the collision. The roster nevertheless remains an exposure that increased risk. It places every haul truck operator at the wheel of a 220 tonne vehicle in the small hours of the tenth to fourteenth consecutive night, where the defence against an unlit hazard at an unlisted intersection is the operator's own detection and response. At an intersection with a longer sight line than RL 312, a slower response could be the difference between stopping and not.

Fatigue of the operator on the night was also examined and could not be settled. For it, the operator was on night 10 of 14 and 8 hours 47 minutes into the shift inside the circadian low. The operator's voluntary sleep record shows between 5 and 7 hours on each of the preceding ten days, and the operator described being tired "the way you are on night ten". The task on the approach was detection in an unlit pit, which fatigue degrades first. Against it, the operator described the tiredness as ordinary, "Not falling asleep tired", and said they were awake and driving properly. Every limit in the standard was met, and the recorded 1.4 second response and the braking and steering showed none of the usual signs. The evidence is evenly balanced on whether the operator was fatigued to a degree that degraded performance, and it could not be resolved without a detailed fatigue assessment, which was not pursued because even a response time of zero ends in a collision at about 17 km/h. Nothing from this matter is carried into the conclusions.

Airborne dust on the ramp above the intersection

Airborne dust was examined as a possible reason the beacon was picked out late. It is likely that dust was present on the ramp above the grade break during the approach. The last water cart pass on that section was 1 hour 37 minutes before the collision against a standing interval of 90 minutes, so a pass was 7 minutes overdue. The fixed dust monitor on the RL 328 bench, 180 m up-ramp of the intersection and above the grade break, logged PM10 at 142 micrograms per cubic metre in the 02:40 to 02:50 interval against a shift mean of 88. The truck operator described dust hanging around, and said the cart had been through earlier and it dries out. The light vehicle driver was firm that the air was clear, but that was at the spur below the windrow, slow or stopped, and not on the ramp above the crest where the truck was.

Whether dust affected the truck operator's sighting could not be settled, and the evidence is evenly balanced on it. In favour, dust hanging in the truck's lights over the crest is the condition in which a driver picks out a beacon late. Against, the reading of 142 is well below the site trigger of 250 and measures particulate at a monitor head and not what could be seen from either cab, and nothing at Bindarra measures visibility. The beacon was in view from 53 m, the geometric limit the survey gives, so a sighting at that limit leaves dust little to explain. The operator declined to say dust made a difference, and a 1.4 second response from that point leaves no room for a delay to hide in. The sighting is inferred from the last steady data point and the survey and was not recorded, so a loss of a fraction of a second at the edge of the lights cannot be excluded. What would settle it is [NOT ESTABLISHED: any measurement of visibility from the cab on the night]. Dust is not treated as a contributing factor, and nothing from this matter is carried into the conclusions.

Night shift extrication

The night shift is rostered with one qualified mines rescue paramedic at the surface medical facility. The second responder, who must be present before any extrication is begun, is called in from the accommodation village 11 km from the gatehouse in the second response vehicle, which carries the hydraulic rescue tool. Dispatch paged the team at 02:48. The first response vehicle entered the pit at 02:51 and reached the scene at 02:54, the second responder arrived with the tool at 03:07, and the driver was extricated at 03:14, 27 minutes after the collision. The post-incident review found the extrication delayed by approximately 9 minutes, measured from 02:58 to 03:07, and recorded that the delay did not affect the clinical outcome because the injuries were stable and the patient was conscious throughout.

The collision and its injuries were complete before the response was paged, so the response time had no path to this outcome, and it is unlikely that it influenced the occurrence. The arrangement is nonetheless a structural exposure on every night shift, because the extrication capability depends on one person plus a drive from the village and does not change with the severity of the casualty. It is very likely that this increased risk. The clinical weight of such a delay in a different casualty condition was not examined, and is [NOT ESTABLISHED: the clinical weight of any extrication delay in a different casualty condition].

What could not be determined

The extent to which dust affected the truck operator's sighting could not be determined, because no measurement of visibility from either cab exists and the sighting is inferred and not recorded. The light vehicle's movements before it reached the spur mouth could not be determined beyond the driver's own account, because the vehicle carried no fleet management system and its tag is passive, so its movements are known only from the proximity log, the account and the scene evidence.

Conclusions

These findings are made with respect to the occurrence and should not be read as apportioning blame or liability to any organisation or individual.

Findings

  1. The available sight distance at the RL 312 spur intersection was 41 m, against a stopping distance of 96 m for a 220 t class truck travelling empty at the posted 40 km/h, and BIN-TMP-004 clause 6.2 required not less than the stopping distance and in no case less than 120 m. This very likely contributed to the collision because it limited the first sight of the light vehicle's beacon to 53 m and left the truck unable to stop short of the spur.
  1. Neither the haul truck operator nor the light vehicle driver made a positive call on the pit channel before the intersection. BIN-TMP-004 clause 4.3.2 required no call there because the spur was not listed at Appendix B. A call from either vehicle would have been heard by the other, by dispatch and by the night shift supervisor, so the absence of a call likely contributed, although a call gives knowledge and not separation.
  1. The light vehicle drove out of the spur onto the ramp without stopping. The driver said they slowed at the mouth, looked up the ramp, saw nothing and drove out, and did not believe they had come to a complete stop. The truck was already within the 38 m the driver could see from the mouth, so a full stop and a second look would very likely have shown it and let it pass, although a stop is only as good as the look from it.
  1. Neither driver was aware of the other until the truck came over the crest, and this was very likely the case, because the light vehicle's movements before the spur mouth rest on the driver's own account alone. The first sight available to the truck operator was the beacon at 53 m, six seconds before impact, and the collision very likely followed directly from the vehicles converging unseen.
  1. The front left of the haul truck struck the right side of the light vehicle at 24 km/h, 6.2 m into the ramp from the spur mouth. This was the mechanism by which the convergence became an injury, and it contributed with virtual certainty.
  1. The light vehicle was pushed 18.4 m down the ramp and rolled onto its left side against the inner windrow. The driver sustained a fractured left clavicle, three fractured left ribs and a small pneumothorax. The roll-over protection structure was deformed but not breached and the seatbelt was fastened. The roll-over was virtually certain to have produced these injuries.
  1. The RL 312 spur was opened under works order WO-26-4471, classified as routine earthworks under ORR-PRO-022 clause 5.3, so no management of change record was raised and none of the three referrals that clause 5.4 requires was made. Of the fourteen new Stage 4 roads cut since the last plan review, the three raised under a management of change record were referred to the plan's owner and none of the eleven raised under a works order was. This very likely contributed by leaving the intersection without controls and inside a suppression geofence. (Safety issue)
  1. The RL 312 intersection had no stop control, warning sign, delineation or posted speed, although clause 6.2 required a stop control, signalised control or traffic controller where the sight distance could not be achieved. Clause 6.4 signage applied only to intersections on the plan's road layout drawing, which did not include the spur. The absence of controls likely contributed. A stop at the mouth would have held the light vehicle while the truck came into view, although the margin from 38 m was thin and the effect of a sign on the truck rests on the operator's own account. (Safety issue)
  1. BIN-TMP-004 required a positive call only at the nine intersections listed at Appendix B and allowed an intersection to be added only at the annual review, with no route for a new road to reach the plan's owner between reviews. The spur was on neither Appendix B nor Schedule 1. This very likely contributed because the operator called at every listed intersection passed that night, the last 51 seconds before the collision, and a call at the spur would very likely have been made had it been listed. (Safety issue)
  1. The collision awareness system was suppressed at the spur by the S4-LOAD geofence, which had been extended up the main ramp on 09/06/2026 without review against the traffic management plan, and operators had not been told. This was very likely the case, because the operator and the night shift supervisor each said they did not know, and no training covers the geofences. The suppression likely contributed, and that judgement is held at the standard of proof and no higher. It worked through expectation, because an operator who believed the system would sound had one less reason to think a light vehicle could be on the ramp. An unsuppressed alert would have sounded about half a second after the beacon came into view and added little, and the effect of the expectation cannot be measured. (Safety issue)
  1. Access cards were issued at the gatehouse against the contractor's recognition agreement with no check for the Bindarra light vehicle pit driving assessment, which ORR-STD-009 clause 7.4 required of every person driving in an operating pit. The light vehicle driver held no such assessment. This likely contributed to the driver leaving the spur without stopping, because the assessment teaches approaching a mouth that cannot be seen out of, although the driver already applied its first rule, and the content of the assessment is [NOT ESTABLISHED: the content of the Bindarra light vehicle pit driving assessment]. (Safety issue)
  1. Mines Safety Guideline MSG-14 clause 3.2 set no definition of a significant change and no review trigger, and clause 5.1 set no basis for nominating the positive-call intersections. This likely contributed because it made inaction the default for a site-owned plan. Bindarra's plan met the guideline on its face, the mine was not in breach, and the mine could have reviewed or listed more intersections on its own under clause 9.1. (Safety issue)
  1. The contractor's Stage 4 haul roster of fourteen consecutive 12 hour 30 minute night shifts placed the operator on night 10 of 14, 8 hours 47 minutes into the shift, with every limit of the fatigue standard met. This unlikely contributed to the collision because the recorded response of 1.4 seconds was inside the 1.5 seconds the plan assumes, and a response time of zero would still have ended in a collision at about 17 km/h. It likely increased risk because the exposure is built into the roster. (Safety issue)
  1. The night shift was rostered with one mines rescue paramedic, and the second responder, required before any extrication, was called in from the village 11 km from the gatehouse. The extrication was delayed by approximately 9 minutes waiting for the second responder and the tool. This unlikely contributed to the occurrence or its outcome because the injuries were complete before the response was paged and the driver was stable and conscious throughout, but it very likely increased risk because the arrangement does not change with the severity of a casualty. (Safety issue)
  1. The haul truck operator braked and steered right within 1.4 seconds of the beacon coming into view, which with virtual certainty occurred. This very likely reduced risk because braking from 37 to 24 km/h removed about 58 per cent of the impact energy, and steering towards the wall kept the push running down the ramp and away from the open edge.
  1. The ramp surface was very unlikely to have been wet or slippery. No rain fell on the night, the surface was dry on examination, and the braked deceleration matched the truck's dry figure.
  1. The service brakes were very unlikely to have delivered less than their tested deceleration. Tests on 03/08/2026 and 14/08/2026 gave 0.80 and 0.82 m/s2 net, and the occurrence download gave 0.78 m/s2.

Recommendations

This section records the safety action already taken and the recommendations made against the safety issues the investigation established. Each recommendation is addressed to an organisation by its role, and the response dates and Open status are as recorded.

Management of change for road network works

The procedure for management of change, ORR-PRO-022, excluded routine earthworks under a works order from the requirement for a management of change record. WO-26-4471 therefore cut the RL 312 spur into a haul road without referral to the traffic management plan owner, the survey department for the fleet management system road network, or the contractor's technical services group for the collision awareness system geofences. Of the 14 new roads cut in Stage 4 since the 12/11/2025 review, 3 raised under a management of change record were referred and none of the 11 raised under a works order was.

Recommendation, addressed to the operator, that clause 5.3 of ORR-PRO-022 stop excluding earthworks that create a new intersection with a haul road, or that the works order form at Schedule 4 carry the three referrals the management of change record holds at clause 5.4. The Investigator in charge made the recommendation. It is Open, with a response due 30/09/2026. [NOT ESTABLISHED: current status of this recommendation]

Traffic management plan: listing of intersections and referral of new roads

Appendix B of BIN-TMP-004 required positive calls only at nine listed intersections, and an intersection could reach the appendix only through the road layout drawing at Schedule 1, which was reissued only at the annual review. The plan did not require a new road to be referred to its owner. The RL 312 spur was on neither document, and the next date on which it could have been listed was 12/11/2026, three months after the collision.

Recommendation, addressed to the operator, that BIN-TMP-004 provide a route by which an intersection reaches Appendix B between annual reviews, and that the plan require a new road to be referred to its owner when it is opened to traffic. The Investigator in charge made the recommendation. It is Open, with a response due 30/09/2026. [NOT ESTABLISHED: current status of this recommendation]

Safety action taken: the Mining Manager, Orrabinda Resources, issued a site-wide direction at 05:10 on 12/08/2026, two hours twenty-three minutes after the collision. It requires a positive call on the pit channel before entering any intersection in the Stage 4 pit, listed in the plan or not, until further notice. The direction was read at the following four pre-starts and posted beside the Appendix B board in the Stage 4 crib room. It is in force and stands until BIN-TMP-004 is amended. It addresses the issue in part, because it requires calls at every Stage 4 intersection for now, but it does not change the plan, so the route to Appendix B between reviews and the referral of new roads are still unprovided.

Suppression geofences on the collision awareness system

The S4-LOAD suppression geofence was moved 180 m up-ramp on 09/06/2026 as a system configuration task. Nobody outside the group that moved it was told, and no training record anywhere on site, for any person, covers the geofences.
